## Motivation {#motivation}

A prediction may require several transformations of the input before a useful output can be produced.
A neural network organises those transformations into a function whose adjustable values can be learned from data.
This note starts with feedforward networks; it separates what the network computes from how its parameters are learned.

## Feedforward neural network {#feedforward-neural-network}

A **feedforward neural network** is a [parameterised function]{.term key="parameterised-function"} organised into layers, with computation flowing from the input toward the output without feedback cycles.
For fixed parameters and deterministic operations, it maps an input to an output; the architecture specifies a family of possible functions, and the chosen parameters select one member.

A **layer** is a stage that transforms its inputs into another set of values.
Its output is a [representation]{.term key="representation"} passed to later computation.
The network output need not be a probability: its meaning depends on the task and the final transformation.

## Layer composition {#layer-composition}

For a simple dense network with one hidden layer, let $x\in\mathbb R^d$ be the input and $h\in\mathbb R^m$ the hidden representation:

$$
  h=\phi(W_1x+b_1),\qquad f_\theta(x)=W_2h+b_2.
$$

Here, $W_1\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, $b_1\in\mathbb R^m$, $W_2\in\mathbb R^{k\times m}$, and $b_2\in\mathbb R^k$ give an output in $\mathbb R^k$.
The symbol $\theta$ collects these [parameters]{.term key="parameter"}, and $\phi$ is an activation function, typically nonlinear and applied coordinatewise in this example.
The formula specifies a forward computation; it does not itself choose a loss or update parameters.

Without a nonlinearity between these two affine transformations, their composition is another affine transformation.
Adding such a layer therefore does not by itself enlarge the family beyond affine functions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: two affine layers collapse to one"}

Set $\phi(u)=u$ and substitute the first layer into the second:

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  f_\theta(x)&=W_2(W_1x+b_1)+b_2\\
  &=(W_2W_1)x+(W_2b_1+b_2).
  \end{aligned}
$$

The combined weight is $W_2W_1$ and the combined bias is $W_2b_1+b_2$.
This is again affine in $x$.

:::

## Example and use {#examples}

As a constructed scalar example, take $h=\max(0,2x-1)$ and $f(x)=3h$.
The hidden layer suppresses inputs at or below $1/2$; above that threshold the output increases with slope $6$.
The same operations and parameters apply to every input, while the intermediate value changes with the input.
Training would adjust the coefficients against a chosen objective; evaluating the formula with fixed coefficients is prediction.

## Connections and boundaries {#connections}

[Loss](loss.qmd#loss-and-risk) defines the penalty used to assess predictions, while [optimisation](../mathematics/optimization.qmd#gradient-descent) changes parameters to reduce an objective.
[Representations](representations.qmd) explains how intermediate values encode information for later use.
[Attention](attention.qmd) is another way to construct transformations; a dense layer is not the definition of every neural-network layer.
A feedforward computation has no feedback cycle within that computation, but the same network can still be called repeatedly by an external controller or generation procedure.
The architecture alone does not establish accuracy, generalisation, or a physical interpretation for a hidden coordinate.

## References

[Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville, *Deep Learning*, Chapter 6](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/mlp.html) develops feedforward networks, composition, and nonlinear hidden units.
